unit.title: What Kind of Word Is It?
unit.summary: What do Christians mean when they call the Bible "the Word of God"? This unit looks at Jesus as the Word and Scripture as the witness to him, the Greek words logos and rhema, what 2 Timothy 3:16 actually says about inspiration, the debate over inerrancy and infallibility, and the history of sola Scriptura, giving each tradition a fair hearing.

lessons.title: Scripture and the Word of God
lessons.question: Is the Bible the Word of God, or is Jesus the Word of God? What is the difference between Scripture and the Word?
lessons.bigIdea: In the New Testament, the Word of God in its fullest sense is a person: Jesus Christ. Scripture is God's gift that bears witness to him. We read the Scriptures to meet the Word, and we let the Word who became flesh show us how to read the Scriptures.

sections.heading: One phrase, several meanings
sections.body:
Many Christians use "the Word of God" and "the Bible" as if they meant exactly the same thing. In the Bible itself the phrase is wider. Sometimes it means God's creative speech: God speaks and the world comes to be (Gen 1:3; Ps 33:6). Sometimes it means a prophetic message: "the word of the LORD came to" Jeremiah or to John the Baptist (Jer 1:4; Luke 3:2). Sometimes it means the preached gospel: "the word of God increased" as the apostles preached (Acts 6:7; 1 Thess 2:13).

Sometimes it does mean written Scripture. Jesus tells the Pharisees that their tradition cancels "the word of God", meaning the commandment in the Law (Mark 7:13), and he says "the Scripture cannot be broken" in the same breath as "the word of God came" (John 10:35). So Scripture can rightly be called the word of God.

And once, at the very centre, the Word is a person. "In the beginning was the Word… and the Word became flesh" (John 1:1; John 1:14). The rider on the white horse is named "The Word of God" (Rev 19:13). No book had ever been called that. When the New Testament reaches for its highest use of the phrase, it points to Jesus.

sections.heading: John 1: the Word who explains the Father
sections.body:
John opens his Gospel by echoing Genesis: "In the beginning". The Greek word for "Word" is *logos*. Jewish readers would hear the Hebrew idea of God's *dabar*, the word that creates and acts (Isa 55:11), and the figure of Wisdom who was with God at creation (Prov 8:22-31). Greek readers would hear *logos* as the reason or order behind the universe. John takes both and says: this Word is not an idea or a principle. He is a person, he was with God, he was God, and he "became flesh and dwelt among us".

John ends the prologue with a striking verb. "No one has ever seen God; the only begotten God, who is at the Father's side, has made him known" (John 1:18). "Made him known" is the Greek *exēgeomai*, the root of our word "exegesis" (careful explanation of a text). Jesus is the Father's own exegesis. Hebrews says the same thing in different words: God spoke "in many portions and in many ways" through the prophets, but "in these last days" he has spoken "in his Son", the exact imprint (*charaktēr*) of his nature (Heb 1:1-3).

This does not make the earlier words false. Hebrews calls them God's speaking. But it does put them in order. The prophets spoke truly and in part; the Son is the full and final word.

sections.heading: John 5:39-40: searching the Scriptures and missing the Word
sections.body:
Jesus says to some of the most devoted Bible students of his day: "You search the Scriptures because you think that in them you have eternal life; and it is they that bear witness about me, yet you refuse to come to me that you may have life" (John 5:39-40). He does not say the Scriptures are unimportant. He says they are a witness. Their job is to point beyond themselves to him.

After the resurrection Jesus does the same thing on the road to Emmaus. "Beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself", and later he "opened their minds to understand the Scriptures" (Luke 24:27; Luke 24:44-45). The risen Jesus is both the subject of Scripture and the one who unlocks it.

This is the root of the learner's phrase: "Jesus is the Word of God through which we interpret the Scriptures." Martin Luther said something close to it when he called Scripture the manger in which Christ is laid: we value the manger because of who lies in it.

sections.heading: Rule book or witness?
sections.body:
If the Bible is read mainly as a rule book, every verse becomes a rule of equal weight. Then polygamy, slavery laws, holy war commands and food laws all sit on the same level as "love your enemies", and readers either try to obey everything (which no one actually does) or pick and choose without saying why. History shows the danger: crusades, the defence of slavery and many acts of violence were justified by quoting Scripture. The learner's notes say it sharply: without the Word, Jesus, the Bible can become deadly.

If the Bible is read as a witness, the question changes. A witness is trusted because it tells the truth about someone. Its parts do different jobs: story, law, poetry, prophecy, letter. Each is asked: what does this show me about God as he is finally seen in Jesus? Jesus himself read this way. He said Moses allowed divorce "because of your hardness of heart" (Matt 19:8), and he set his own word beside the older commands ("You have heard that it was said… but I say to you", Matt 5:38-44).

The two pictures are not completely opposed. Witnesses can contain commands, and the New Testament does give instruction (2 Tim 3:16-17). The difference is about the centre: is the centre a list of rules, or a person to whom every page points?

sections.heading: How different traditions put it
sections.body:
Almost all Christians agree that Jesus is the Word made flesh and that Scripture is God-given. They differ on how closely to tie the two. Karl Barth taught a "threefold form" of the Word of God: the Word revealed (Jesus Christ), the Word written (Scripture), and the Word proclaimed (preaching). For Barth the written word becomes God's Word to us when God speaks through it. Many evangelicals, following B. B. Warfield, say the opposite emphasis is needed: Scripture is God's Word in itself, because "what Scripture says, God says", whether or not we hear it.

Catholic teaching (Vatican II, *Dei Verbum* 2-4 and 21) says that Christ is the fullness of revelation and that the Church venerates the Scriptures as it venerates the Lord's body. Orthodox Christians hear the Gospel book carried in procession and kissed, because in it Christ speaks to his people. Both hold Scripture and Christ close together without confusing them.

The learner's view, that Scripture bears witness to the Word and is not the Word himself, stands near Barth and the Christ-centred readers listed in this course. The safeguard every tradition adds is this: the Jesus we use as the key must be the Jesus the Scriptures actually present, not a Jesus we have shaped to our liking.

views.name: Jesus is the Word; Scripture is the witness
views.who: Karl Barth; Brad Jersak; Brian Zahnd; Greg Boyd; Peter Enns; Tommy Miller; in older forms Luther ('what promotes Christ')
views.summary: The Word of God in the full sense is Jesus. Scripture is inspired and authoritative because it bears witness to him. Every passage is read with Jesus as the key, so that a picture of God unlike Jesus is a sign we have misread.
views.strengths: Follows the New Testament's own highest use of 'the Word' (John 1; Rev 19:13) and Jesus' teaching that the Scriptures testify to him (John 5:39). Guards against using isolated verses as weapons.
views.critiques: Jesus himself called written Scripture 'the word of God' and 'unbreakable' (Mark 7:13; John 10:35). Critics ask who decides what is 'Christlike', and warn that the Jesus used as a key can become our own ideal. Supporters answer that the key is the Jesus of the Gospels, cross and resurrection, which is public and checkable.

views.name: Scripture is the Word of God written
views.who: B. B. Warfield; J. I. Packer; John Stott; the Chicago Statement (1978); much evangelical and Reformed teaching
views.summary: Jesus is the living Word and Scripture is the written Word. Both are fully God's speech. Because Jesus treated the Scriptures as God speaking (Matt 19:4-5), Christians should too. What Scripture says, God says.
views.strengths: Takes seriously how Jesus and the apostles quoted Scripture. Gives a stable, public authority that does not depend on the reader's feelings.
views.critiques: Can flatten Scripture into a rule book where every verse weighs the same. Barthians and Christ-centred readers say it risks putting the book where only Christ belongs. Defenders answer that the living and written Word never compete, because Christ himself authorised the Scriptures.

views.name: Scripture within the living Tradition
views.who: Catholic teaching (*Dei Verbum*, 1965); Orthodox theologians such as Georges Florovsky
views.summary: Christ is the fullness of revelation. Scripture is the inspired witness to him, received, interpreted and proclaimed within the church that wrote it down and recognised it. Word, Scripture and church belong together.
views.strengths: Explains historically how the Bible came to us through a worshipping community. Keeps Christ, Scripture and the church in one picture.
views.critiques: Protestants worry that the church's interpretation can end up above Scripture. Catholic and Orthodox writers answer that the church serves the Word and does not stand over it (*Dei Verbum* 10).

misreadings.topic: "The Word of God" always means the Bible
misreadings.popular: When a verse mentions 'the word of God', it means the 66-book Bible we hold today, so verses like Heb 4:12 or Isa 55:11 describe the printed book.
misreadings.inContext: The first hearers had no bound Bible. 'Word of God' meant God's spoken word, a prophetic message, the Law, or the preached gospel, and in John and Revelation it is a title of Jesus. Scholars across traditions (for example Raymond Brown on John, Craig Koester on Revelation) note this range.
misreadings.defence: Evangelical scholars agree the phrase has a range, but stress that Jesus did call written Scripture 'the word of God' (Mark 7:13; John 10:35), so applying these verses to Scripture is legitimate by extension. Both sides can agree: Scripture is one form of God's word, and Jesus is its centre.
misreadings.whyItMatters: If every mention of 'the word' means 'the book', we can lose sight of the person the book is about, as Jesus warned in John 5:39-40.

discuss: Before this lesson, when you heard 'the Word of God', what did you picture? Has that changed?
Jesus told Bible experts that they searched the Scriptures but would not come to him (John 5:39-40). How could that happen today?
What is the difference between treating the Bible as a rule book and as a witness? Can you name a real example of each?
Barth says Scripture becomes God's Word when God speaks through it; Warfield says it is God's Word whether or not we listen. What does each view protect?
If Jesus is the key to Scripture, how do we make sure the 'Jesus' we use is the real one and not our own ideal?
practice: Read John 1:1-18 slowly three times. Each time, note one thing it says about the Word that could not be said about a book.
Each time you read the Bible this week, ask at the end: what did this show me about Jesus, or what does Jesus show me about this?
Look up five places where 'word of God' or 'word of the LORD' appears and write down which meaning each one has.

lessons.title: Rhema and Logos
lessons.question: What is the difference between rhema and logos? Is rhema a personal 'now word' and logos the written Word?
lessons.bigIdea: Logos and rhema are both ordinary Greek words for 'word', and the New Testament uses them in overlapping ways. The experience many Christians call 'a rhema word' is real and important, but it cannot be proved from the Greek words alone.

sections.heading: Two Greek words for 'word'
sections.body:
The New Testament has two common nouns that English Bibles usually translate as "word". *Logos* (about 330 uses) comes from the verb *legō*, "to say". It can mean a word, a statement, a message, an account, a reason, or a matter being discussed. *Rhēma* (about 68 uses) comes from a root meaning "to speak". It usually means something spoken: a saying, an utterance, a word. Like the Hebrew *dabar*, it can also mean "a thing" or "a matter" (Luke 2:15).

Both words appear in the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint, or LXX) to translate the same Hebrew word *dabar*. That already tells us the translators did not see them as two different kinds of revelation. Standard lexicons such as BDAG (the main scholarly Greek-English dictionary of the New Testament) list wide and overlapping meanings for both.

sections.heading: The popular distinction
sections.body:
In many Pentecostal and charismatic churches you will hear: "The *logos* is the written Word, the whole Bible, general and for everyone. A *rhema* is a specific word the Holy Spirit speaks to you, now, for your situation." A Bible verse "becomes rhema" when it leaps off the page and you know God is saying it to you.

This teaching was spread widely by David Yonggi Cho, pastor of the Yoido Full Gospel Church in Seoul, in *The Fourth Dimension* (1979). He pointed to Rom 10:17 ("faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word", where the Greek is *rhēma*) and to Peter walking on the water at Jesus' specific command. Earlier, W. E. Vine's *Expository Dictionary* (1940) had commented that the "sword of the Spirit, which is the word (*rhēma*) of God" (Eph 6:17) refers not to the whole Bible as such but to the particular scripture the Spirit brings to mind when it is needed. Watchman Nee, Bill Hamon and others taught similar ideas, and the distinction became common in Word of Faith teaching.

The experience behind it is widely shared. Many believers describe a moment when a familiar verse suddenly spoke to them with personal force. Jesus himself fought temptation with specific scriptures at the right moment (Matt 4:4). The question is not whether God speaks personally. It is whether the two Greek words carry that difference.

sections.heading: What the texts actually show
sections.body:
When we look at every use, the neat division breaks down. *Logos* is often a specific spoken word for a specific moment, exactly what the popular teaching calls rhema. The centurion says to Jesus, "only say the word (*logos*), and my servant will be healed" (Matt 8:8). Jesus tells the disciples, "You are already clean because of the word (*logos*) I have spoken to you" (John 15:3). And the verse most often quoted about the living, piercing power of God's word uses *logos*, not *rhēma* (Heb 4:12).

In the other direction, *rhēma* is often general and public, not private. God "upholds all things by the word (*rhēma*) of his power" (Heb 1:3). The universe was formed by the *rhēma* of God (Heb 11:3). Peter quotes Isaiah, "the word (*rhēma*) of the Lord remains forever", and adds, "this is the word (*rhēma*) that was preached to you" (1 Pet 1:25), just two verses after calling the same message the living and abiding *logos* (1 Pet 1:23). In Rom 10:8 Paul's *rhēma* is "the word of faith that we proclaim": the public gospel, not a private impression.

So most Greek scholars conclude that the two words overlap heavily and are often interchangeable, with *rhēma* tending slightly toward "something said" and *logos* tending toward "message" or "account". This is a point on which evangelical, Catholic and secular scholars largely agree.

sections.heading: Why word studies can mislead
sections.body:
In 1961 James Barr's *The Semantics of Biblical Language* warned against a common habit: treating each Greek or Hebrew word as if it carried a whole theology inside it. Words get their meaning from how they are used in sentences, not from their roots or from a theory about them. D. A. Carson's *Exegetical Fallacies* (1984) and Moisés Silva's *Biblical Words and Their Meaning* (1983) gave many examples. Building a doctrine on a supposed difference between two synonyms is one of the classic mistakes they describe.

This does not mean the charismatic experience is wrong. It means that if Christians want to speak of God giving a personal, timely word, they should base it on texts that actually describe that (John 10:27; John 14:26; Acts 13:2), not on the vocabulary of *rhēma*. Pentecostal scholars such as Gordon Fee, in *The Disease of the Health and Wealth Gospels* (1985), have likewise urged their own movement to build on careful reading of texts in context rather than on slogans.

Two safeguards are shared by both sides. A personal word never contradicts the public word about Jesus (Gal 1:8). And any 'word' should be tested in the community (1 Thess 5:19-21; 1 Cor 14:29).

views.name: Rhema as a personal, Spirit-given word
views.who: David Yonggi Cho (*The Fourth Dimension*, 1979); Bill Hamon; Watchman Nee; many Word of Faith and charismatic teachers; drawing on W. E. Vine
views.summary: Logos is God's general, written revelation. Rhema is the Spirit applying a word to a person at a particular moment, which births faith (Rom 10:17) and becomes a weapon in spiritual battle (Eph 6:17).
views.strengths: Names a real experience of many believers: a verse that suddenly speaks with personal force. Encourages expectancy that God speaks today and that Scripture is not dead letters.
views.critiques: The Greek usage does not support the division (Matt 8:8; Heb 1:3; Heb 4:12). Critics warn that it can set private impressions above the public Scripture. Some holders answer that they use the terms as convenient labels for an experience, not as a claim about Greek grammar.

views.name: Synonyms with slight shades
views.who: Most Greek lexicographers and New Testament scholars (BDAG; James Barr; Moisés Silva; D. A. Carson)
views.summary: Logos and rhema overlap heavily and are often interchangeable. Rhema leans slightly toward 'something said', logos toward 'message' or 'account', but context decides the meaning, not the word chosen.
views.strengths: Built on every use of both words, including the Septuagint. Protects against building doctrine on a single word.
views.critiques: Can sound as if it dismisses personal guidance. Holders reply that they affirm God's personal speaking but ground it in other texts (John 10:27; Acts 13:2).

views.name: Logos as message, rhema as its spoken moment
views.who: Some careful pastoral writers and teachers who modify the popular view
views.summary: Both words describe God's word, but rhema often highlights the act of speaking, so it can fittingly describe Scripture heard and received in the moment. The distinction is a tendency, not a rule.
views.strengths: Keeps what is true in the popular teaching while respecting the evidence.
views.critiques: Even as a tendency it has many counter-examples (Heb 1:3; 1 Pet 1:23). Scholars warn that a tendency is easily turned into a rule again in preaching.

misreadings.topic: Rhema is the word for a personal revelation
misreadings.popular: When the Bible says rhema, it means a personal, present word from God; when it says logos, it means the written Scriptures. So Rom 10:17 teaches that faith comes from hearing a personal rhema.
misreadings.inContext: In Rom 10:8-17 Paul's rhema is 'the word of faith that we proclaim': the public message about Jesus carried by sent preachers. Faith comes by hearing that message. Lexicons (BDAG) and scholars such as Douglas Moo and James Dunn read the verse this way.
misreadings.defence: Charismatic scholars agree the passage is about preaching, but note that preaching is itself God speaking through a human voice now (1 Thess 2:13). So the heart of the experience, God speaking in the present, can stand even if the word-distinction does not.
misreadings.whyItMatters: If faith depends on getting a private rhema, believers who have never had such an experience may doubt their faith. Paul grounds faith in the public gospel available to all.

discuss: Have you ever had a verse 'come alive' for you in a specific moment? How would you describe that experience without using the words logos and rhema?
Why do you think the logos/rhema teaching became so popular?
What risks come from building a doctrine on one Greek word? Can you think of other examples?
How should a personal word from God be tested? What role do Scripture and the church play?
Jesus answered temptation with written Scripture spoken at the right time (Matt 4:4). What does that suggest about how the Bible and the Spirit work together?
practice: Using an interlinear Bible or app, look up five verses with 'word' and find whether the Greek is logos or rhema. Did the context decide the meaning?
Memorise one verse this week, so that it is ready for the Spirit to bring to mind (John 14:26).
If you sense God speaking to you through a verse, write it down and share it with a mature friend, and ask: does this agree with the Jesus of the Gospels?

lessons.title: God-Breathed: What 2 Timothy 3:16 Says
lessons.question: Does it say "All Scripture is God-breathed" or "Every God-breathed Scripture is useful"? Is it talking about the whole Bible or the Old Testament? Did the Holy Spirit write the Bible?
lessons.bigIdea: 2 Timothy 3:16 was written about the Jewish Scriptures Timothy knew from childhood, and it says they are God-breathed and useful for forming God's people. Inspiration in the Bible's own picture is not dictation: God breathed through human authors, carrying them along, so that their words give life.

sections.heading: The Greek and the grammar question
sections.body:
The Greek of 2 Tim 3:16 begins *pasa graphē theopneustos kai ōphelimos pros didaskalian*. Word for word: "every / all" (*pasa*), "scripture" (*graphē*), "God-breathed" (*theopneustos*), "and" (*kai*), "useful" (*ōphelimos*), "for teaching". There is no word for "is" in the sentence. Greek often leaves it out, so the translator has to decide where to put it.

Option one: "All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful" (KJV, NIV, ESV and most modern versions). Here both adjectives describe Scripture equally. Option two: "Every God-breathed Scripture is also useful" (the Latin Vulgate, Tyndale, the Revised Version of 1881, the American Standard Version of 1901). Here *theopneustos* describes which scripture is meant, and the main claim is that it is useful.

Most grammarians prefer option one. The main reason: when two adjectives are joined by "and" (*kai*) like this, they are normally both doing the same job; option two has to read *kai* as "also", which is possible but less natural. The best-known parallel is 1 Tim 4:4, "every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected", where the same pattern is read as two statements. But option two is a real grammatical possibility, which is why several careful versions chose it or put it in the margin (the NRSV margin reads "Every scripture inspired by God is also useful").

sections.heading: Does the choice change much?
sections.body:
Some readers fear that option two implies some Scripture is not God-breathed. That is not the natural meaning. In context Paul has just reminded Timothy of "the sacred writings" he has known from childhood (2 Tim 3:15). "Every God-breathed Scripture" would describe those writings as a class, not pick out some and reject others. Either way, Paul assumes the Scriptures are God-breathed.

The real difference is emphasis. Option one makes a statement about the nature of Scripture: it is God-breathed. Option two stresses its purpose: because it is God-breathed, it is useful "for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness, so that the person of God may be complete, equipped for every good work" (2 Tim 3:16-17). Even with option one, the sentence's goal is practical. Paul is not writing a doctrine of the Bible; he is telling a young pastor why to keep going back to Scripture in hard times.

sections.heading: Which 'Scripture' did Timothy have?
sections.body:
When Paul wrote, there was no New Testament as a collection. "The sacred writings" Timothy learned from his Jewish mother Eunice and grandmother Lois (2 Tim 1:5; Acts 16:1) were Israel's Scriptures: the Law, the Prophets and the Writings. As a Greek-speaking Jew of Asia Minor he most likely knew them in the Greek translation called the Septuagint (LXX). So the first meaning of 2 Tim 3:16 is about what Christians now call the Old Testament.

But the New Testament already shows the idea widening. 2 Pet 3:15-16 places Paul's letters alongside "the other Scriptures". 1 Tim 5:18 introduces two quotations with "the Scripture says": one is Deut 25:4, the other matches words of Jesus found in Luke 10:7. Christians later applied 2 Tim 3:16 to the whole Bible by this same logic: the apostolic witness to Christ belongs with Israel's Scriptures.

So the learner's question has a two-part answer. Historically, Paul was speaking of the Jewish Scriptures. Theologically, the churches have extended his words to the New Testament, on grounds the New Testament itself begins to give.

sections.heading: Theopneustos: God-breathed, inspired, life-giving
sections.body:
*Theopneustos* appears only here in the Bible. It joins *theos* (God) and a form of *pneō* (to breathe; compare *pneuma*, breath or spirit). The Latin Vulgate rendered it *divinitus inspirata*, "divinely breathed into", which gave us the English word "inspiration". In 1900 B. B. Warfield argued that the word means "breathed out by God": Scripture is the product of God's breath, like his creative word (Ps 33:6). That is why the NIV and ESV say "God-breathed" and "breathed out by God".

A minority of scholars read it more actively, as "God-breathing" or "life-giving": Scripture breathes God's life into its readers. John C. Poirier's *The Invention of the Inspired Text* (2021) argues that early uses of the word outside the Bible usually meant "life-giving". Critics such as Craig Keener reply that Jewish talk of inspired Scripture consistently implied its authority and truth, and that the context of 2 Tim 3:16 fits Warfield's reading. Most scholars still follow Warfield on the basic sense.

Either way, the word echoes Gen 2:7, where God breathed the breath of life into the man formed from dust and he became a living being. The learner's note fits this echo well: inspiration is not God replacing the human author, but God breathing into a human work so that it carries his life. Ezekiel's dry bones live when breath enters them (Ezek 37:9-10), and the risen Jesus breathes on his disciples as he sends them (John 20:22).

sections.heading: Did the Holy Spirit write the Bible?
sections.body:
The Bible's clearest description of how prophecy came is 2 Pet 1:21: "no prophecy was ever produced by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit." "Carried along" (*pheromenoi*) is the word Luke uses for a ship driven by the wind (Acts 27:15). The sailors are still on board and still working; the wind sets the direction.

The human authors are visible everywhere. Luke did research and interviewed eyewitnesses (Luke 1:1-4). Paul forgets whom he baptised (1 Cor 1:16) and separates what the Lord commanded from his own counsel (1 Cor 7:10-12). The psalmists write in grief and anger; each writer has his own vocabulary and style. As the learner wrote, God never bypassed human involvement.

So most Christian traditions answer: yes, the Spirit is the ultimate author, and no, the Spirit did not write it the way a typist takes dictation. Christians do not hold the view many Muslims hold of the Qur'an, as words sent down without a human author's personality. The Bible is fully the word of its human writers and, in the way each tradition explains, the word of God.

sections.heading: Theories of inspiration
sections.body:
Christians have described inspiration in several ways. Dictation: God gave the very words and the writer recorded them. Some early writers used images like a musician playing an instrument (Athenagoras, *Plea for the Christians* 9), but almost no major tradition today holds strict dictation. Verbal plenary inspiration: God so guided the writers that the words themselves (verbal) in every part (plenary) are what he intended, while the writers' personalities and styles remain; Warfield called this God's "concursus" with the human authors. Dynamic or thought inspiration: God inspired the writers and their ideas, and they chose the words.

The incarnational analogy (Herman Bavinck earlier; Peter Enns in *Inspiration and Incarnation*, 2005): as Jesus is fully divine and fully human, so Scripture is fully God's word and fully human, shaped by its ancient culture. Encounter or neo-orthodox views (Karl Barth, Emil Brunner): Scripture is a human witness that becomes God's Word when God speaks through it. Catholic teaching (*Dei Verbum* 11) holds that God is the author and the human writers are "true authors" too, using their own powers.

These views overlap more than they compete. Each tries to hold two facts together: God speaks, and humans wrote. They differ on how close the link is between God's intention and the exact human words.

views.name: Verbal plenary inspiration
views.who: B. B. Warfield; J. I. Packer; John Stott; most conservative evangelicals
views.summary: All Scripture, Old and New Testament, is breathed out by God in its very words, through human authors whose personalities God used. 2 Tim 3:16 states the nature of Scripture, not only its usefulness.
views.strengths: Fits the most natural grammar of 2 Tim 3:16 and the way Jesus quoted Scripture as God's speech (Matt 19:4-5). Explains why Christians can trust Scripture's details.
views.critiques: Critics say it can drift toward dictation in practice and struggles with the human, culturally shaped features of the text. Defenders reply that concursus explicitly affirms the human authors and that they never taught dictation.

views.name: Incarnational inspiration
views.who: Peter Enns; Kenton Sparks; drawing on Herman Bavinck and Chrysostom's idea of God's 'condescension'
views.summary: God breathed through real people in real cultures; Scripture is fully human and fully God's word, as Christ is fully human and divine. Its ancient features are not embarrassments but the way God chose to speak.
views.strengths: Takes the human features seriously (Luke 1:1-4; 1 Cor 7:10-12) and fits the learner's 'God never bypassed human involvement'.
views.critiques: Critics (e.g. G. K. Beale) say the analogy is used to accept errors, while Christ's humanity was without sin. Supporters answer that being culturally located is not the same as sin.

views.name: Inspiration as God breathing life (encounter)
views.who: Karl Barth; Emil Brunner; with a related reading of theopneustos as 'life-giving' (John C. Poirier)
views.summary: Scripture is a human witness to God's revelation in Christ. It is inspired because the Spirit breathed on its writing and still breathes through it to give life, making it God's Word to us.
views.strengths: Highlights the life-giving purpose of Scripture (2 Tim 3:15-17; John 6:63) and keeps Christ at the centre.
views.critiques: Evangelicals say it makes Scripture's status depend on the event of hearing, and the 'life-giving' reading of theopneustos is a minority view. Barthians reply that God's speaking, not our hearing, is what makes it God's Word.

views.name: Dual authorship within the Church
views.who: Catholic teaching (*Dei Verbum* 11-13); Orthodox writers in their own idiom
views.summary: God is the author of Scripture and the human writers are true authors. The Spirit who inspired Scripture also guides the Church that reads it.
views.strengths: Holds divine and human authorship together and explains how Scripture is received within a community.
views.critiques: Protestants worry about the Church's role in interpretation; some critical scholars think 'author' language is unclear. Catholic theologians answer that the Church's role is service, not control.

misreadings.topic: Inspiration means God dictated the Bible
misreadings.popular: God told each writer exactly what to write, word by word, so the human writers added nothing of their own.
misreadings.inContext: The Bible shows human research (Luke 1:1-4), personal memory (1 Cor 1:16), emotion and distinct styles. 2 Pet 1:21 pictures humans speaking while carried by the Spirit, like a ship in the wind. Scholars of every tradition agree that inspiration works through human authorship.
misreadings.defence: Conservative evangelical scholars agree: Warfield, Packer and the Chicago Statement (Article VIII) reject mechanical dictation and affirm that God used the writers' personalities. Their claim is that God's work through the writers was so complete that the result is still fully his word.
misreadings.whyItMatters: A dictation picture makes people either ignore the human features of Scripture or lose faith when they notice them.

misreadings.popular: Paul is saying the whole Bible, Genesis to Revelation, is God-breathed.
misreadings.inContext: Paul was describing the Jewish Scriptures Timothy knew from childhood (2 Tim 3:15), probably in Greek. Much of the New Testament had not yet been written or collected.
misreadings.defence: Evangelical scholars accept this but argue that the principle rightly extends to the New Testament, since the New Testament already places apostolic writings beside Scripture (2 Pet 3:16; 1 Tim 5:18). Catholic and Orthodox Christians also extend it, by the Church's recognition of the canon.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Knowing the first meaning helps us see how Jesus and the apostles valued Israel's Scriptures, and how the church came to treat its own writings the same way.

lessons.title: Inerrant? Infallible?
lessons.question: Is the Bible inerrant and infallible? What do those words mean, and do all Christians agree?
lessons.bigIdea: "Inerrant" means without error in what it affirms; "infallible" means it will not fail in its purpose. Christians hold a range of views on how far these words apply, and each view is trying to honour both God's truthfulness and the human, ancient shape of the text.

sections.heading: Two words, carefully defined
sections.body:
First a spelling note: the word is "inerrant" (from Latin *in-* "not" and *errare* "to wander, to err"), not "inherent". *Inerrancy* means that Scripture contains no errors in what it affirms. *Infallibility* means that Scripture cannot fail or mislead in what it sets out to do. In older writing the two words were often used as synonyms. Since the 1960s and 1970s they have often been used to mark a difference: some say Scripture is infallible in its saving purpose but not necessarily inerrant in every historical or scientific detail.

The Bible does not use either word about itself. The concepts are drawn from what it says about God and his word: God does not lie (Num 23:19; Titus 1:2; Heb 6:18), "every word of God proves true" (Prov 30:5), "your word is truth" (John 17:17), and Jesus said "Scripture cannot be broken" (John 10:35). The disagreement is about how to apply those truths to a text written by many people in many cultures over about 1,500 years.

sections.heading: The Chicago Statement and full inerrancy
sections.body:
In October 1978 about 300 evangelical leaders, meeting as the International Council on Biblical Inerrancy, signed the *Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy*: 19 articles of affirmation and denial, with an exposition. It affirmed that Scripture "in its entirety is inerrant, being free from all falsehood, fraud, or deceit" (Article XII), including in its statements about history and science. Signers included J. I. Packer, R. C. Sproul, Francis Schaeffer and James Montgomery Boice. It followed a decade of debate, including Fuller Seminary's 1972 revision of its statement of faith and Harold Lindsell's book *The Battle for the Bible* (1976).

The statement is more careful than its critics sometimes say. It applies inerrancy to the original manuscripts (the autographs). It says inerrancy is not broken by lack of modern technical precision, irregular grammar, round numbers, descriptions of nature as they appear to the eye ("the sun rose"), loose quotations, or the reporting of falsehoods (Satan's words are accurately recorded, not endorsed). And it rejects dictation (Article VIII). Interpreting genre correctly is part of the doctrine.

Defenders argue that a God who cannot lie would not breathe out a text that errs, and that Jesus treated details of the Old Testament as reliable (Matt 5:18; Matt 12:40). They add that once errors are admitted, there is no clear place to stop.

sections.heading: Limited inerrancy and infallibility of purpose
sections.body:
Other evangelicals hold that Scripture is fully truthful and trustworthy in all it teaches about God, salvation, faith and life, while allowing that some incidental details of history, numbers or science may reflect the limited knowledge of the human writers. This is sometimes called "limited inerrancy" or "infallibility". It was held by scholars such as Daniel Fuller and I. Howard Marshall, and by the Lausanne Covenant's wording (1974) that Scripture is "without error in all that it affirms", which both sides could sign.

People in this view point to features they think are better handled honestly: Mark 2:26 names Abiathar as high priest where 1 Sam 21:1-6 names Ahimelech; Matt 27:9 attributes to Jeremiah a quotation that is mostly from Zechariah (Zech 11:12-13); numbers in Kings and Chronicles sometimes differ (2 Sam 24:9; 1 Chr 21:5). Inerrantists offer explanations for each (for example, that Matthew blends Zechariah with Jeremiah's field-buying in Jer 32:6-9, citing the more prominent prophet). Readers should look at both and judge.

The Catholic Church's Vatican II teaching, *Dei Verbum* 11 (1965), says that the books of Scripture teach "without error that truth which God wanted put into sacred writings for the sake of salvation". Catholic scholars debate whether that phrase limits inerrancy to saving truth or describes all of Scripture as serving that purpose.

sections.heading: Orthodox, Barthian and incarnational views
sections.body:
Eastern Orthodox Christians rarely use the word "inerrancy". They receive Scripture as the inspired heart of the church's Tradition, true and trustworthy as read in the worshipping church with the Fathers. The modern Protestant debate about scientific and historical precision is largely foreign to them; the question they ask is whether a reading agrees with the church's faith in Christ.

Karl Barth held that Scripture is a fully human witness that can err in its human words, yet God freely chooses to speak his Word through it. For Barth, the Bible's authority rests on God's speaking, not on a theory of the text. Peter Enns' incarnational model says that God accommodated himself to ancient ways of writing history and describing the world. He argues that this is like Jesus taking real, limited human flesh, and that judging the Bible by modern standards of precision is itself a mistake about genre.

The early church often spoke of God's *synkatabasis* (condescension, coming down to our level), as John Chrysostom did. *Dei Verbum* 13 uses this idea too. In different ways, Orthodox, Barthian and incarnational writers all draw on it.

sections.heading: Critiques in both directions, and where it touches the Jesus lens
sections.body:
Critiques of strict inerrancy: it can turn a statement about God's faithfulness into a test of fellowship; it applies to manuscripts no one has; and it can push readers to defend a text by forced harmonising instead of listening to it. Some, such as Christian Smith, argue it leads to "biblicism" that still produces endless disagreement. Many people who lose faith describe an all-or-nothing view: one problem text and the whole structure fell.

Critiques of limited inerrancy and the other views: who decides which parts are "incidental"? If the Bible can be wrong about history, can it be wrong about the resurrection, which is a historical claim (1 Cor 15:14-17)? Inerrantists also note that Jesus treated Scripture as fully reliable, so a lower view sets the disciple above the teacher.

The learner's Jesus-lens view fits this debate in a particular way. It holds that Scripture is wholly trustworthy in bringing us to Christ (John 5:39; 2 Tim 3:15), and that the Old Testament honestly records a developing and sometimes partial human perception of God. Greg Boyd (*Inspired Imperfection*, 2020) argues that the Bible's imperfections are part of how God humbly accommodated himself to his people, letting their limited pictures of him stand in the text, and that this enhances rather than weakens its authority. Others in this camp prefer "infallible in purpose", and some Christ-centred readers still hold a form of inerrancy. Critics reply that this asks the reader to sort true pictures of God from false ones in the text, which is exactly what inerrancy is meant to prevent.

views.name: Full (Chicago) inerrancy
views.who: J. I. Packer; R. C. Sproul; Al Mohler; D. A. Carson; Norman Geisler
views.summary: Because God cannot lie and Scripture is God-breathed, Scripture is true in all that it affirms, including history, when it is read according to its genre and intent.
views.strengths: Follows from God's character and from Jesus' high view of Scripture (Matt 5:18; John 10:35). Gives a stable foundation and resists cultural pressure to edit the Bible.
views.critiques: Applies to autographs we do not have; can encourage forced harmonising; can make faith brittle. Defenders answer that the copies are extremely reliable and that honest explanations exist for most problem texts.

views.name: Infallibility / limited inerrancy
views.who: I. Howard Marshall; Daniel Fuller; many British evangelicals; Jack Rogers and Donald McKim (historical argument)
views.summary: Scripture is fully trustworthy and never fails in its purpose of bringing us to God in Christ and teaching faith and life. Small incidental details may reflect the human writers' limits.
views.strengths: Deals openly with human features. Rogers and McKim argued it fits how many earlier theologians, such as Calvin, spoke of accommodation.
views.critiques: John Woodbridge answered Rogers and McKim that the church fathers and Reformers did hold to full truthfulness. Critics ask who decides what is incidental, and note the resurrection is a historical claim.

views.name: Catholic teaching
views.summary: God is the author of Scripture and the human writers are true authors. Scripture teaches without error the truth God wanted recorded for our salvation, and is interpreted within the Church's living Tradition.
views.strengths: Holds divine and human authorship together, and connects truth to God's saving purpose.
views.critiques: Catholic scholars themselves debate whether 'for the sake of salvation' limits inerrancy. Protestants worry that interpretation depends on the Magisterium.

views.name: Orthodox and Barthian approaches
views.who: Georges Florovsky; Theodore Stylianopoulos; Karl Barth
views.summary: Different routes to a shared instinct: Scripture's authority lies in God's self-revelation in Christ, received in the church (Orthodox) or in God's free speaking (Barth), rather than in a theory of the text's precision.
views.strengths: Avoids tying faith to every detail. Keeps Christ at the centre.
views.critiques: Evangelicals say these views leave the text's truthfulness unclear. Barth is criticised for separating God's Word too far from the words of Scripture.

views.name: Jesus-lens / incarnational
views.who: Peter Enns; Greg Boyd; Brad Jersak; Eric Seibert
views.summary: Scripture is trustworthy in bearing witness to Christ. The Old Testament includes honest records of people's developing, partly mistaken perceptions of God; Jesus is the measure by which all is read.
views.strengths: Explains why some pictures of God in the Old Testament seem unlike Jesus, while keeping all of Scripture as inspired and useful.
views.critiques: Critics (e.g. Paul Copan, Carson) say it lets readers choose which texts reflect God, risks a Marcion-like split, and sits uneasily with Jesus' own acceptance of the Old Testament. Holders answer that Jesus himself corrected earlier understandings (Matt 5:38-44; Matt 19:8).

misreadings.popular: If the Bible is inerrant, every statement must be taken literally, so poetry like 'the trees clap their hands' or 'the sun rises' must be literal claims.
misreadings.inContext: Biblical writers used poetry, parable, round numbers and everyday description. Reading genre correctly is basic to understanding any text, including Isa 55:12 and Ps 19:4-6.
misreadings.defence: The Chicago Statement itself (Articles XIII and XVIII) says inerrancy must be applied through careful grammatical and historical interpretation that takes account of literary forms. Inerrantist scholars agree that literalism is not inerrancy.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Confusing the two makes inerrancy look foolish to critics and makes believers defend things the Bible never claimed.

misreadings.popular: Anyone who does not hold Chicago-style inerrancy is a liberal who does not believe the Bible.
misreadings.inContext: Many who believe in the resurrection, the miracles and the authority of Scripture use 'infallible' instead of 'inerrant', including Orthodox Christians, many Catholics and many British evangelicals. The term became a dividing line in the American debates of the 1970s.
misreadings.defence: Inerrantists answer that they do not call such people liberals, but believe their position is unstable and tends to drift over time. Both sides can agree that a person's view of inerrancy is not the measure of their faith in Christ.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Labelling fellow believers can split churches over a term the Bible does not use.

discuss: Before this lesson, what did you think 'inerrant' meant? What do you think now?
Why might a person's faith depend on believing in perfect accuracy? Why might another person's faith be helped by a less strict view?
Look at Mark 2:26 and 1 Sam 21:1-6. How do different views handle them?
What does Jesus' statement that 'Scripture cannot be broken' (John 10:35) mean in its context?
Can Christians who disagree on inerrancy still fully trust the Bible? What would that look like?
How does reading Scripture through Jesus affect how you think about these questions?

lessons.title: Sola Scriptura: A History
lessons.question: Where did 'Scripture alone' come from? Did the Reformers mean 'just me and my Bible'? How do Catholics and Orthodox see tradition?
lessons.bigIdea: Sola Scriptura was the Reformers' claim that Scripture is the only infallible rule, the final judge over all church teaching. It did not mean ignoring the church, the creeds or the Fathers. Catholics and Orthodox answer that Scripture is always received within the church's living Tradition.

sections.heading: Before the Reformation: Scripture and tradition together
sections.body:
In the early church, Scripture and the apostolic tradition were seen as one stream. Paul tells the Thessalonians to "hold to the traditions that you were taught by us, either by our spoken word or by our letter" (2 Thess 2:15) and praises the Corinthians for keeping the traditions he delivered (1 Cor 11:2). Against the Gnostics, Irenaeus of Lyon (about 180) appealed both to Scripture and to the faith publicly handed down in the churches founded by apostles (*Against Heresies* 3.3-4). Basil of Caesarea defended some practices as unwritten apostolic traditions (*On the Holy Spirit* 27).

Around 434, Vincent of Lérins gave a famous test for true teaching: hold to what has been believed "everywhere, always, and by all" (*Commonitorium* 2). This "Vincentian canon" is still quoted by Catholics, Orthodox and Anglicans. Vincent also said Scripture is sufficient in itself; tradition was needed because people interpret it in so many ways.

In the late Middle Ages the question sharpened. John Wycliffe in England (died 1384), in *On the Truth of Holy Scripture* (1378), argued that Scripture is the highest authority for the church and that popes can be judged by it. Jan Hus in Prague took up similar ideas and was burned at the Council of Constance in 1415. Historian Heiko Oberman described two medieval positions: "Tradition I" (Scripture as the one source, interpreted in the church) and "Tradition II" (Scripture and unwritten tradition as two sources).

sections.heading: Luther and the Reformers: Scripture as the final judge
sections.body:
At the Leipzig Debate in 1519 Johann Eck pressed Martin Luther until he said that church councils can err. At the Diet of Worms in April 1521, asked to recant, Luther said in substance that unless he was convinced by Scripture and plain reason, since popes and councils had often erred and contradicted each other, his conscience was captive to the Word of God. The famous words "Here I stand" may have been added in later printed versions.

The Reformers' principle came to be called *sola Scriptura*, "by Scripture alone". It meant that Scripture is the only infallible authority, the norm that judges every other authority ("the norming norm"). The Formula of Concord (1577) calls Scripture "the only rule and norm"; the Westminster Confession (1646) ch. 1 calls the Spirit speaking in Scripture the "supreme judge" of all controversies, and adds that Scripture interprets Scripture (1.9).

It did not mean rejecting tradition. Luther and Calvin quoted the Fathers constantly, kept the ancient creeds, and saw themselves as recovering the early church. Lower authorities such as creeds, councils and teachers were real authorities, but they were always answerable to Scripture. The Bereans who checked Paul's teaching against the Scriptures (Acts 17:11) and Jesus' rebuke of traditions that cancel God's command (Mark 7:8-13) were favourite texts.

sections.heading: The responses: Trent, the Anabaptists and 'solo scriptura'
sections.body:
The Catholic Council of Trent replied in its fourth session (8 April 1546). It taught that the truth of the gospel is contained "in the written books and the unwritten traditions" received from Christ and the apostles, and that both are to be received with equal devotion and reverence. It also named the canon (including the deuterocanonical books) and said no one should interpret Scripture against the sense held by the Church.

On the other side, some Radical Reformers went further than Luther and Calvin. Many Anabaptists (for example the Swiss Brethren of the Schleitheim Confession, 1527) read the New Testament directly in small communities, and rejected infant baptism partly because they did not find it in Scripture. Some spiritualists placed the inner Spirit above the outer word. Modern writers such as Keith Mathison, using Oberman's terms, call the attitude that rejects all church tradition and leaves each individual with "me and my Bible" *solo scriptura* (or "Tradition 0"), to distinguish it from the magisterial Reformers' *sola*. Mathison's labelling of the Anabaptists is itself debated; Anabaptist scholars stress that they read Scripture together, in community, under Christ.

The difference matters. *Sola* says Scripture is the final authority, read with the church. *Solo* says Scripture is the only authority and each person is their own interpreter. Many critics of Protestantism, including Catholic and Orthodox writers and Christian Smith (*The Bible Made Impossible*, 2011), point to the thousands of Protestant groups as the fruit of *solo* reading.

sections.heading: Anglicans, Wesley and prima scriptura
sections.body:
The Church of England's Thirty-Nine Articles (1571) say Scripture contains all things necessary for salvation (Article VI) and that the church may not ordain anything contrary to it (Article XX). Richard Hooker's *Laws of Ecclesiastical Polity* (from 1594) gave Scripture first place, then reason, then the church's tradition. Later writers pictured this as a "three-legged stool", though the image is not Hooker's own.

John Wesley called himself "a man of one book" yet also used tradition, reason and Christian experience. In 1964 the Methodist scholar Albert Outler coined the term "Wesleyan quadrilateral" for this pattern: Scripture, tradition, reason and experience. Outler later regretted the term, because people took it to mean four equal sources. In Wesley, Scripture was primary and the others helped to interpret it.

This position is often called *prima Scriptura*: Scripture first, but not alone in the sense of the only source of insight. Many Pentecostals and charismatics also live this way in practice, holding Scripture supreme while expecting the Spirit to speak through experience and prophecy, tested by Scripture (1 Thess 5:21).

sections.heading: Catholic and Orthodox views of Tradition today
sections.body:
Vatican II's *Dei Verbum* (1965) softened the language of "two sources". It says Tradition and Scripture "flow from the same divine wellspring" and form one sacred deposit of the word of God entrusted to the Church (§§9-10). The Church's teaching office (the Magisterium) interprets it, but "is not above the word of God, but serves it" (§10). Catholics point to 1 Tim 3:15, which calls the church "a pillar and buttress of the truth", and to the fact that the church recognised the canon itself.

Eastern Orthodox Christians speak of Holy Tradition as the life of the Holy Spirit in the church. Scripture is the highest expression of that Tradition, not a separate source competing with it. Georges Florovsky and Vladimir Lossky stressed that Scripture is read rightly in worship, with the Fathers and the councils, as the mind of the church. For the Orthodox, setting Scripture against Tradition is like setting a person's words against their life.

Protestant responses vary. Some argue that Tradition has added doctrines not found in Scripture (for example later Marian dogmas), which is exactly what *sola Scriptura* was meant to test. Others, especially in recent "retrieval" movements, have rediscovered the Fathers and creeds as a gift for reading Scripture well, while keeping Scripture as the final judge.

views.name: Magisterial sola Scriptura
views.who: Martin Luther; John Calvin; Lutheran and Reformed confessions; Keith Mathison; Kevin Vanhoozer
views.summary: Scripture is the only infallible rule of faith and the final judge of all teaching. The church, creeds and Fathers are real but fallible authorities under it.
views.strengths: Follows Jesus' practice of judging traditions by Scripture (Mark 7:8-13) and the Bereans (Acts 17:11). Gives a way to reform the church when it goes wrong.
views.critiques: Catholics and Orthodox ask who decides what Scripture means and point to Protestant division. They also note the canon itself was recognised by the church. Reformers answer that the church recognised, not created, the canon, and that unity under error is worse than division.

views.name: Prima Scriptura
views.who: Richard Hooker; John Wesley; Albert Outler; many Anglicans, Methodists and Pentecostals
views.summary: Scripture is the primary authority, interpreted with the help of tradition, reason and experience, none of which may overrule it.
views.strengths: Describes honestly how most Christians actually read. Values the Spirit's present work and the wisdom of the past.
views.critiques: Critics say that in practice experience or culture can quietly become the real authority. Supporters reply that Wesley always kept Scripture first.

views.name: Scripture and Tradition (Catholic)
views.who: Council of Trent (1546); *Dei Verbum* (1965); Joseph Ratzinger
views.summary: Scripture and Tradition flow from one source, Christ, and together form one deposit of faith. The Magisterium serves the word of God by interpreting it faithfully.
views.strengths: Explains how the canon and creeds came to be and provides a clear way to settle disputes (Acts 15). Fits 2 Thess 2:15.
views.critiques: Protestants argue that some doctrines rest on Tradition without clear scriptural basis and that in practice the Magisterium has the last word. Catholics answer that it is bound by Scripture and Tradition and cannot invent doctrine.

views.name: Scripture within Holy Tradition (Orthodox)
views.who: Georges Florovsky; Vladimir Lossky; Kallistos Ware
views.summary: Tradition is the life of the Holy Spirit in the church; Scripture is its summit and heart, read in worship with the Fathers and the councils.
views.strengths: Reads Scripture as the church's book, in prayer and liturgy, as the first Christians did. Avoids pitting Bible and church against each other.
views.critiques: Protestants ask how Tradition can be corrected if it errs. Orthodox reply that the Spirit preserves the church and that the councils themselves were guided by Scripture.

misreadings.popular: Sola Scriptura means we just read the Bible for ourselves and do not need creeds, church history or the Fathers.
misreadings.inContext: The Reformers kept the ancient creeds, quoted the Fathers and wrote confessions. Sola Scriptura made Scripture the final judge, not the only resource. Historians such as Heiko Oberman and theologians such as Keith Mathison call the individualist version 'solo scriptura'.
misreadings.defence: Those in free-church traditions answer that they do honour the past, but want each generation to test everything by Scripture directly, as the Bereans did (Acts 17:11). Both sides agree that reading in community is wiser than reading alone.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Reading without the wider church makes it easy to read our own assumptions into the text, the problem of eisegesis studied in Lesson 10.

misreadings.topic: Catholics and Orthodox do not value Scripture
misreadings.popular: Catholics and Orthodox put tradition above the Bible and do not really read it.
misreadings.inContext: Catholic and Orthodox liturgies read large amounts of Scripture aloud; the Psalms are prayed daily in monasteries. *Dei Verbum* 21-25 urges all believers to read Scripture, quoting Jerome: ignorance of Scripture is ignorance of Christ.
misreadings.defence: Protestant scholars accept this and focus their critique on authority, not devotion: when Scripture and Tradition seem to differ, which decides? That is the real disagreement.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Caricatures block honest conversation between Christians who share the same Scriptures and creeds.
